                 ORDER INSTITUTING PROCEEDINGS PURSUANT TO
              SECTION 6(c) AND (d) OF THE COMMODITY EXCHANGE ACT,
              MAKING FINDINGS, AND IMPOSING REMEDIAL SANCTIONS

                                          I.        INTRODUCTION

        The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“Commission”) has reason to believe that
from January 2019 through June 2023 (“Relevant Period”), UBS Financial Services Inc.
(“Respondent” or “UBS FSI”) violated Commission Regulation (“Regulation”) 166.3, 17 C.F.R.
§ 166.3 (2025). Therefore, the Commission deems it appropriate and in the public interest that
public administrative proceedings be, and hereby are, instituted to determine whether
Respondent engaged in the violations set forth herein and to determine whether any order should
be issued imposing remedial sanctions.

       In anticipation of the institution of an administrative proceeding, Respondent has
submitted an Offer of Settlement (“Offer”), which the Commission has determined to accept.
Respondent admits the facts set forth in Section II below, acknowledges that its conduct violated
Regulation 166.3, consents to the entry of this Order Instituting Proceedings Pursuant to Section
6(c) and (d) of the Commodity Exchange Act, Making Findings, and Imposing Remedial
Sanctions (“Order”), and acknowledges service of this Order.1




1
 Respondent agrees to the use of the findings of fact and conclusions of law in this Order in this proceeding and in
any other proceeding brought by the Commission or to which the Commission is a party or claimant, including but
not limited to, a proceeding in bankruptcy or receivership, and agrees that they shall be taken as true and correct and
be given preclusive effect therein, without further proof. Respondent does not consent, however, to the use of this
Order, or the findings or conclusions herein, as the sole basis for any other proceeding brought by the Commission
or to which the Commission is a party or claimant, other than: a proceeding in bankruptcy or receivership; or a
proceeding to enforce the terms of this Order.

                                        II.    FINDINGS

The Commission finds the following:

A.     SUMMARY

        During the Relevant Period, UBS FSI, a registered futures commission merchant
(“FCM”), failed to adequately configure and administer its anti-money laundering (“AML”)
transaction monitoring systems for wire transfers that were denominated in foreign currencies
and effectuated through retail customer accounts. Through this conduct, UBS FSI failed to
diligently supervise activities related to its business as an FCM in violation of Regulation 166.3.

        Customers of UBS FSI were able to utilize accounts opened for commodities or securities
trading to transfer foreign currency (“FX”). Specifically, they could send FX from and receive
FX into retail customer commodity accounts via wire transfers. Due to deficiencies in UBS
FSI’s configuration of the relevant surveillance tools and data governance practices, thousands of
FX wires sent or received through retail customer commodity accounts held at UBS FSI were
either insufficiently monitored or omitted from transaction monitoring for AML compliance. As
these failures reflect, UBS FSI lacked a reasonably designed process for subjecting FX wires
transmitted through retail customer commodity accounts to AML transaction monitoring.

       In accepting Respondent’s Offer, the Commission acknowledges Respondent’s
representations concerning its remediation in connection with this matter.

B.     RESPONDENT

       UBS Financial Services Inc. is a registered FCM with its principal place of business
located in Weehawken, New Jersey. UBS FSI has been registered with the Commission as an
FCM since 1982.

C.     FACTS

       1.      UBS FSI Failed to Diligently Supervise Its Manual and Automated
               Surveillance Systems for FX Wires.

        As an FCM, UBS FSI has an affirmative duty to diligently supervise its business by,
among other things, establishing and implementing reasonable controls to monitor transactions to
detect and report suspicious activity. Beginning prior to January 2019 and continuing to
February 2021, UBS FSI used a manually-generated report to monitor FX wire transactions sent
or received by retail commodity accountholders for suspicious activity. The manual report was
deficient, as it failed to capture all relevant FX wires for monitoring and was not tailored to
identify patterns of suspicious activity in FX wire transactions. UBS FSI was aware of these
vulnerabilities because it was the subject of prior enforcement proceedings by other government
agencies and a self-regulatory organization. In resolving those earlier proceedings, UBS FSI
represented in 2018 that it would address the deficiencies in the manual surveillance process by
implementing an automated AML transaction monitoring system by mid-2019. Despite those

                                                 2

representations, UBS FSI continued to rely on the manual report system for two years after the
2018 settlements.

        In 2021, UBS FSI transitioned to using an automated system to monitor all wire
transactions conducted through retail accounts at the firm, including FX wires, for suspicious
activity. UBS FSI, however, failed to properly configure the data flowing into the new system,
causing issues that impacted the efficacy of its suspicious activity monitoring function.
Accordingly, the deficiencies in UBS FSI’s AML transaction monitoring program span both a
portion of time when the manual report was still in use, and a more recent period of time during
which the new automated system was in use.

        Overall, due to these issues, UBS FSI estimates that more than 28,000 FX wires
effectuated through retail customer commodity accounts with a total U.S. dollar value of at least
$8.9 billion were insufficiently monitored or omitted from AML transaction monitoring during
the Relevant Period.

               a.      UBS FSI Failed to Timely Correct Known Deficiencies in Its Manual
                       Surveillance Report.

        Beginning prior to January 2019 and continuing until February 2021, UBS FSI utilized a
manually-generated report to capture inbound and outbound FX wire transfers conducted
through retail customer commodity accounts. As UBS FSI knew from the December 2018
enforcement proceedings by other agencies referenced above, the report was not reasonably
designed to detect and cause the reporting of suspicious transactions occurring in connection
with retail customer commodity accounts. The report suffered from three primary deficiencies in
its design and execution, as detailed below.

        First, while the report was intended to generate surveillance alerts for FX wires transacted
through retail customer commodity accounts, it was not reasonably tailored to address money
laundering risks. The parameters that the report applied to wire data to generate alerts focused
only on the volume of the FX wires and the notional value and type of currency involved in each
transaction. The manual report did not capture a range of suspicious activity detection scenarios,
such as transfers to/from high-risk jurisdictions, round dollar transactions, suspicious payment
instructions, deviation of actual behavior from expected behavior, velocity of funds movement
across products, or activity in dormant accounts. UBS FSI understood at the time that the
manual report did not identify those types of activities. It further understood that only an
automated solution would provide comprehensive monitoring capabilities. Despite those known
deficiencies and its 2018 representations in connection with the resolution of the prior
enforcement actions that it would implement a new system by mid-2019, UBS FSI took more
than two years after the 2018 settlements to implement an automated system. This delayed
implementation led to significant gaps in its AML surveillance of FX wires during the
intervening period.

       Second, the firm’s process for manually collecting and marrying data from multiple
sources to produce the data set for the report lacked adequate documentation. The process
required UBS FSI personnel to query as many as four different data systems to compile a list of

                                                 3

all FX wires transacted through retail customer commodity accounts for a given period;
manually search for customer identification information and relevant account numbers associated
with the transactions; and then subject the compiled wire data files to a set of coded queries. The
process involved significant data cleanup work, and its manual nature could result in input errors.
UBS FSI also did not maintain official written supervisory procedures that documented the
process for compiling the report or the individuals responsible for the report as part of its
governance or AML programs.

        Third, the report was generally reviewed on a quarterly basis, which led at times to a
series of backlogs. Given the manual nature of the alert generation process, UBS FSI staff did
not execute the report on a more frequent basis. The delays between the wire activity and the
alert generation and review process created the risk that UBS FSI was not positioned to intervene
in a timely manner to address any suspicious activity that was identified.

        Despite being on notice of these deficiencies, UBS FSI failed to timely resolve them.
While UBS FSI originally planned to implement the automated system in 2019, it ultimately did
not deploy that system until March 2021, when it began generating alerts on February 2021
transactions. UBS FSI continued to rely on the manual surveillance report as a compensating
control in the interim period.

        New deficiencies in the manual report also came to light in October 2020, when UBS FSI
discovered a coding error that had prevented certain FX wires from triggering alerts for nearly
the entirety of the prior two years. While UBS personnel were aware at that time that the coding
error affected prior iterations of the report, they took no immediate steps to escalate the issue
upon its discovery or determine the volume of missed alerts. An examination by a self-
regulatory organization later caused UBS FSI to revisit the issue and commence an internal
lookback in December 2020, approximately two months after UBS FSI personnel first
discovered the issue and its effect on prior reports. According to the assessment conducted by
UBS FSI, the manual report process failed to properly generate more than 400 alerts because of
the coding error. After the issue was identified and corrected, UBS FSI did not implement any
quality assurance processes with respect to the coding logic to ensure that the FX report was
functioning as intended for the remaining months of its use.

               b.     UBS FSI’s Flawed Implementation of an Automated AML
                      Transaction Monitoring System for FX Wires Hindered the
                      Effectiveness of Its Surveillance Program.

       Once UBS FSI implemented the automated system for AML transaction monitoring in
March 2021, not all of the relevant FX wires were transferred from source systems to that
platform as intended, and certain wires that did transfer to the platform were missing
counterparty information, affecting monitoring. Accordingly, even after the transition to the
automated system, UBS FSI lacked an effective FX wires surveillance program.

       Many of the missed wires during this period resulted from the fact that UBS FSI
incorrectly configured the system to rely on retail customer commodity account FX wire data
from an intra-day data feed of relevant transactions rather than a complete post-settlement “end-

                                                4

of-day” data feed. As a result of that error, the system ingested an incomplete list of
transactions. In addition, in January 2022, UBS FSI staff changed their practice for labeling FX
wire postings without communicating the change to the staff who handled the processing logic
for the system, and as a result the system’s logic continued to look for the prior labeling practice
and failed to identify certain transactions as FX wires. UBS FSI did not remediate either of these
issues until October 2022, more than a year after the system’s implementation.

       Issues leading to missing counterparty information in the automated system included the
absence of a common identifier (e.g., a wire reference number) to link certain data fields between
account postings and wire files and the incorrect formatting of wire reference numbers and
currency codes.

         These gaps resulted from two key deficiencies in the firm’s data governance practices.
First, prior to the automated system going live, UBS FSI did not subject the key data elements to
a full testing and mapping exercise or certification process. As a result, UBS FSI did not trace
the relevant data points from the system back to their master sources to confirm that they had
been correctly selected for monitoring. Second, until December 2022, UBS FSI did not
implement any kind of exception queue or error reporting mechanism to detect instances when
information pertaining to a wire could not be ingested into the system. For both reasons, UBS
FSI was not equipped to identify gaps or inadequacies in the flow of wire information from
upstream source systems and data feeds to the system. UBS FSI failed to identify these post-
implementation flaws until around May 2022.

       2.      UBS FSI’s Remediation

        UBS FSI has represented that it has undertaken the following remediation. Once UBS
self-identified the data issues in or around May 2022, it voluntarily brought the issues to the
attention of other regulators that were examining its transaction monitoring program for FX
wires at that time. In August 2022, after other government agencies and a self-regulatory
organization had initiated investigations into UBS FSI’s AML transaction monitoring systems
for FX wires, UBS FSI engaged a third-party consultant to evaluate the root causes of the data
issues described above, assess corrective actions, and test the flow of wire-related information to
the automated surveillance system. By the fourth quarter of 2022, UBS FSI remediated the core
data issues that contributed to the FX wire data discrepancies described above. The consultant
has also completed data testing of UBS FSI’s FX wire AML data, issued an initial report, and is
validating UBS FSI’s resolution of the data issues in preparation for producing a final report.
UBS FSI has also established a supervision structure for the handling and oversight of the
relevant transaction data pursuant to its firmwide data management framework.

        UBS FSI further engaged the same consultant to conduct a “lookback” over the
population of FX wires that were either insufficiently monitored or omitted from monitoring
during the Relevant Period due to the above-referenced deficiencies in UBS FSI’s AML
transaction monitoring processes. UBS FSI regularly reported the results of the lookback in
monthly meetings with representatives of the Commission and three other regulators.



                                                 5

        Finally, UBS FSI voluntarily engaged the same consultant to conduct an ongoing “look-
across” data review of other transaction types surveilled by the automated system at issue to
ensure that there are no similar data issues impacting the AML transaction monitoring of other
transaction types.

                                 III.   LEGAL DISCUSSION

A.     UBS FSI Failed to Diligently Supervise Its FX Wires Surveillance System in Violation
       of Regulation 166.3.

           Regulation 166.3, 17 C.F.R. § 166.3 (2025), imposes on every Commission registrant
(except associated persons who have no supervisory duties) an affirmative duty to “diligently
supervise the handling by its partners, officers, employees and agents . . . of all commodity
interest accounts carried, operated, advised or introduced by the registrant and all other
activities of its partners, officers, employees and agents . . . relating to its business as a
Commission registrant.” A violation of Regulation 166.3 is an independent violation for which
no underlying violation is necessary. See, e.g., In re Collins, CFTC No. 94-13, 1997 WL
761927, at *10 (Dec. 10, 1997) (“It is well settled that a violation under Rule 166.3 is ‘an
independent and primary violation for which no underlying violation is necessary.’” (citation
omitted)); In re GNP Commodities, Inc., CFTC No. 89-1, 1992 WL 201158, at *17 n.11 (Aug.
11, 1992) (“Rule 166.3 establishes failure to supervise as an independent and primary violation
. . . .” (citation omitted)), aff’d in relevant part and modified sub nom. Monieson v. CFTC, 996
F.2d 852 (7th Cir. 1993).

        For a registrant to fulfill its duties under Regulation 166.3, it must both design an
adequate program of supervision and ensure that the program is diligently followed. See GNP
Commodities, 1992 WL 201158, at *17-19 (providing that, even if an adequate supervisory
system is in place, Regulation 166.3 can still be violated if the supervisory system is not
diligently enforced). As a result, a violation of Regulation 166.3 “is demonstrated by showing
either that: (1) the registrant’s supervisory system was generally inadequate; or (2) the
registrant failed to perform its supervisory duties diligently.” In re FCStone, LLC, CFTC No.
15-21, 2015 WL 2066891, at *3 (May 1, 2015) (consent order) (citing In re Murlas
Commodities, Inc., CFTC No. 85-29, 1995 WL 523563, at *9 (Sept. 1, 1995)).

        As an FCM, UBS FSI had a duty to design an adequate program of supervision for AML
transaction monitoring and ensure that the program was followed. During the Relevant Period,
UBS FSI failed to fulfill those obligations with respect to its FX wires monitoring program.
UBS FSI was aware of significant vulnerabilities in the manually-generated report system that
hindered the firm’s ability to effectively monitor FX wire transactions effectuated through retail
customer commodity accounts, but failed to reasonably address the vulnerabilities from January
2019 to February 2021. UBS FSI also failed to design adequate policies and procedures to
govern the use of the manually-generated report. In addition, once it switched to an automated
system in approximately March 2021, UBS FSI did not exercise adequate oversight over the
configuration and functioning of that system. UBS FSI therefore violated Regulation 166.3.



                                                6

                            IV.     FINDINGS OF VIOLATIONS

        Based on the foregoing, the Commission finds that, during the Relevant Period, UBS FSI
violated Regulation 166.3, 17 C.F.R. § 166.3 (2025).

                             V.      OFFER OF SETTLEMENT

       Respondent has submitted the Offer in which it knowingly and voluntarily:

A.     Consents to the resolution of this matter in an administrative proceeding;

B.     Acknowledges service of this Order;

C.     Admits the facts described in Section II of this Order and acknowledges that its conduct
       violated Regulation 166.3, 17 C.F.R. § 166.3 (2025);

D.     Admits the jurisdiction of the Commission with respect to all matters set forth in this
       Order and for any action or proceeding brought or authorized by the Commission based
       on violation of or enforcement of this Order;

E.     Waives:

       1.    The filing and service of a complaint and notice of hearing;

       2.    A hearing;

       3.    All post-hearing procedures;

       4.    Any and all rights or defenses that it has or might have for the matter to be
             adjudicated in a federal district court in the first instance, including any associated
             right to a jury trial;

       5.    Judicial review by any court;

       6.    Any and all objections to the participation by any member of the Commission’s
             staff in the Commission’s consideration of the Offer;

       7.    Any and all claims that it may possess under the Equal Access to Justice Act, 5
             U.S.C. § 504, and 28 U.S.C. § 2412, and/or the rules promulgated by the
             Commission in conformity therewith, Part 148 of the Regulations, 17 C.F.R.
             pt. 148 (2025), relating to, or arising from, this proceeding;

       8.    Any and all claims that it may possess under the Small Business Regulatory
             Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, Pub. L. No. 104-121, tit. II, §§ 201–253, 110
             Stat. 847, 857–74 (codified as amended at 28 U.S.C. § 2412 and in scattered
             sections of 5 U.S.C. and 15 U.S.C.), relating to, or arising from, this proceeding;
             and

                                                 7

     9.    Any claims of Double Jeopardy based on the institution of this proceeding or the
           entry in this proceeding of any order imposing a civil monetary penalty or any
           other relief, including this Order;

F.   Agrees for purposes of the waiver of any and all rights under the Equal Access to Justice
     Act specified in Paragraph E.7 above, that Respondent is not the prevailing part in this
     action;

G.   Stipulates that the record basis on which this Order is entered shall consist solely of the
     findings contained in this Order to which Respondent has consented in the Offer;

H.   Consents, solely on the basis of the Offer, to the Commission’s entry of this Order that:

     1.    Makes findings by the Commission that Respondent violated Regulation 166.3, 17
           C.F.R. § 166.3 (2025);

     2.    Orders Respondent to cease and desist from violating Regulation 166.3, 17 C.F.R.
           § 166.3 (2025);

     3.    Orders Respondent to pay a civil monetary penalty in the amount of eight million
           dollars ($8,000,000), plus any post-judgment interest; and

     4.    Orders Respondent and its successors and assigns to comply with the conditions
           and undertakings consented to in the Offer and as set forth in Part VI of this Order;
           and

I.   Represents that it has already engaged in remedial measures relating to its FX wires
     monitoring program, including, but not limited to, the following:

     1.     In August 2022, Respondent engaged a third-party consultant to evaluate the root
            causes of the data issues described above, assess corrective actions, and test the
            flow of wire-related information to the automated surveillance system. The
            consultant has completed the data testing, issued an initial report, and is validating
            Respondent’s resolution of the data issues in preparation for producing a final
            report. Respondent has also established a supervision structure for the handling
            and oversight of the relevant transaction data pursuant to its firmwide data
            management framework;

     2.     Respondent further engaged the same consultant to conduct a “lookback” over the
            population of FX wires that were either insufficiently monitored or omitted from
            monitoring during the Relevant Period due to the above-referenced deficiencies in
            Respondent’s AML transaction monitoring processes; and

     3.     Respondent engaged the same consultant to conduct an ongoing “look-across”
            data review of other transaction types surveilled by the automated system at issue
            to ensure that there are no similar data issues impacting the AML monitoring of
            other money movement transaction types.

                                               8

     Upon consideration, the Commission has determined to accept the Offer.

                                      VI.     ORDER

Accordingly, IT IS HEREBY ORDERED THAT:

A.   Respondent shall cease and desist from violating Regulation 166.3, 17 C.F.R. § 166.3
     (2025).

B.   Respondent shall pay a civil monetary penalty in the amount of eight million dollars
     ($8,000,000) (“CMP Obligation”) within thirty (30) days of the date of the entry of this
     Order. If the CMP Obligation is not paid in full within thirty (30) days of the date of the
     entry of this Order, then post-judgment interest shall accrue on the unpaid portion of the
     CMP Obligation beginning on the date of entry of this Order and shall be determined by
     using the Treasury Bill rate prevailing on the date of entry of this Order pursuant to 28
     U.S.C. § 1961.

     Respondent shall pay the CMP Obligation and any post-judgment interest by electronic
     funds transfer, U.S. postal money order, certified check, bank cashier’s check, or bank
     money order. If payment is to be made other than by electronic funds transfer, then the
     payment shall be made payable to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and sent
     to the address below:

            MMAC/ESC/AMK326
            Commodity Futures Trading Commission
            6500 S. MacArthur Blvd.
            HQ Room 266
            Oklahoma City, OK 73169
            9-amz-ar-cftc@faa.gov

     If payment is to be made by electronic funds transfer, Respondent shall contact the
     Federal Aviation Administration at the above email address to receive payment
     instructions and shall fully comply with those instructions. Respondent shall accompany
     payment of the CMP Obligation with a cover letter that identifies the paying Respondent
     and the name and docket number of this proceeding. The paying Respondent shall
     simultaneously transmit copies of the cover letter and the form of payment to the Chief
     Financial Officer, Commodity Futures Trading Commission, Three Lafayette Centre,
     1155 21st Street, NW, Washington, D.C. 20581.

C.   Respondent and its successors and assigns shall comply with the following conditions
     and undertakings set forth in the Offer:

     1.     Cooperation, in General: Respondent shall cooperate fully and expeditiously with
            the Commission, including the Commission’s Division of Enforcement, and any
            other governmental agency or any self-regulatory organization, in this action, and
            in any current or future Commission investigation or action related thereto.

                                              9

              Respondent shall also cooperate in any investigation, civil litigation, or
              administrative matter related to, or arising from, the subject matter of this action.

       2.     Partial Satisfaction: Respondent understands and agrees that any acceptance by
              the Commission of any partial payment of Respondent's CMP Obligation shall
              not be deemed a waiver of its obligation to make further payments pursuant to this
              Order, or a waiver of the Commission's right to seek to compel payment of any
              remaining balance.

       3.     Change of Address/Phone: Until such time as Respondent satisfies in full its
              CMP Obligation as set forth in this Order, Respondent shall provide written
              notice to the Commission by certified mail of any change to its telephone number
              and mailing address within ten calendar days of the change.

       4.     Notices to Creditors: Until such time as Respondent satisfies in full its CMP
              Obligation, upon the commencement by or against Respondent of insolvency,
              receivership or bankruptcy proceedings or any other proceedings for the
              settlement of Respondent's debts, all notices to creditors required to be furnished
              to the Commission under Title 11 of the United States Code or other applicable
              law with respect to such insolvency, receivership bankruptcy or other
              proceedings, shall be sent to the address below:

                       Secretary of the Commission
                       Office of the General Counsel
                       Commodity Futures Trading Commission
                       Three Lafayette Centre
                       1155 21st Street N.W.
                       Washington, DC 20581


The provisions of this Order shall be effective as of this date.

By the Commission.

              ORDER INSTITUTING PROCEEDINGS PURSUANT TO
       SECTION 6(c) AND (d) OF THE COMMODITY EXCHANGE ACT, MAKING
               FINDINGS, AND IMPOSING REMEDIAL SANCTIONS

                                          I.       INTRODUCTION

        The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“Commission”) has reason to believe that,
from at least 2019 to September 2025 (the “Relevant Period”), Netrios LP Ltd. (“Netrios”)
violated Section 4(a) of the Commodity Exchange Act (“Act”), 7 U.S.C. § 6(a), and Red Acre
Ltd. (“Red Acre”) aided and abetted the violation of Section 4(a), pursuant to section 13(a) of the
Act, 7 U.S.C. § 13c(a). Therefore, the Commission deems it appropriate and in the public
interest that public administrative proceedings be, and hereby are, instituted to determine
whether Netrios and Red Acre (collectively, “Respondents”) engaged in the violations set forth
herein and to determine whether any order should be issued imposing remedial sanctions.

       In anticipation of the institution of an administrative proceeding, Respondents have
submitted an Offer of Settlement (“Offer”), which the Commission has determined to accept.
Without admitting any of the findings or conclusions herein, Respondents consent to the entry of
this Order Instituting Proceedings Pursuant to Section 6(c) and (d) of the Commodity Exchange
Act, Making Findings, and Imposing Remedial Sanctions (“Order”), and acknowledge service of
this Order.1




1
  Respondents consent to the use of this Order’s findings of fact and conclusions of law in this proceeding and in any
other proceeding brought by the Commission or to which the Commission is a party or claimant, and agree that they
shall be taken as true and correct and be given preclusive effect therein, without further proof. Respondents do not
consent, however, to the use of this Order, or the findings or conclusions herein, as the sole basis for any other
proceeding brought by the Commission or to which the Commission is a party or claimant, other than: a proceeding
in bankruptcy or receivership; or a proceeding to enforce the terms of this Order. Respondents do not consent to the
use of the Offer or this Order, or the findings or conclusions in this Order, by any other party in any other
proceeding.

                                      II.    FINDINGS

The Commission finds the following:

A.     SUMMARY

        During the Relevant Period, Respondents conducted business dealing in illegal off-
exchange leveraged or margined retail commodity transactions involving U.S. customers who
were not eligible contract participants (“ECPs”) (as defined in Section 1a(18) of the Act, 7
U.S.C. § 1a(18)) that were required to be made on or subject to the rules of a board of trade,
which had been designated or registered by the Commission as a contract market (i.e., a
designated contract market (“DCM”)). Netrios sold a specialized service that provided the
essential functions for offering and selling leveraged or margined retail commodities through
offshore and off-exchange branded platforms that solicited U.S. customers without regard to ECP
status, otherwise known as “white label” entities (“WLE”). Red Acre intentionally aided and
abetted Netrios’s operations by providing customer and other support, as well as offering
marketing services, to the WLEs. In so doing, Netrios unlawfully engaged in activities that
could only lawfully be performed on a registered DCM, and Red Acre aided and abetted
Netrios’s illegal activities.

B.     RESPONDENTS

       Netrios LP Ltd. is a limited liability company incorporated in Saint Lucia and is the
successor entity of Netrios Ltd., a defunct Dominica company. Neither Netrios nor Netrios Ltd.
has ever been registered with the Commission in any capacity.

       Red Acre Ltd. is a limited liability company incorporated in the Republic of Malta. Red
Acre has never been registered with the Commission in any capacity.

C.     FACTS

        During the Relevant Period, Netrios sold a white label service that provided the
functionality for non-ECP U.S. customers to conduct leveraged or margined retail commodity
transactions through the WLEs. Netrios’s service included the following:

           •   Introducing WLEs to service providers for the purpose of overseas incorporation;
           •   Providing a ready-to-operate website where customers had access to third-party
               trading software that Netrios sub-licensed to the WLEs;
           •   Establishing margin accounts that held customer funds;
           •   Rendering trade execution and liquidity services, and
           •   Performing back-office functions.

The underlying technology and infrastructure that Netrios furnished to each WLE were largely
identical except for the branding, which was provided by the WLE.




                                               2

        Netrios controlled the default products that could be traded through the WLEs.
Leveraged or margined forex transactions comprised the majority of trades. Other products
offered included leveraged or margined precious metals, cryptocurrencies, and equities.

        U.S. customers were permitted to conduct leveraged or margined retail commodity
transactions through the WLEs without regard to their ECP status, using the system created
through the technology and infrastructure that Respondents packaged and sold to the WLEs.
Respondents knew that the WLEs regularly solicited non-ECP U.S. customers, that these U.S.
customers regularly conducted leveraged or margined transactions through the WLEs, and that
none of the WLEs were registered with the Commission in any capacity.

        Typically, an incipient customer would register a trading account on a WLE and transfer
cryptocurrency such as bitcoin, ether, or tether to a WLE margin account at a cryptocurrency
gateway and custodial wallet provider. An affiliate of Respondents owned, in part, this
gateway/wallet provider, and Netrios controlled the WLE margin accounts. Customers
conducted their leveraged or margined retail commodity transactions through the trading
software that was available on the WLE website. None of the transactions involving non-ECP
U.S. customers on the WLE platforms resulted in actual delivery of a commodity within 28 days
of the transaction date. The WLEs charged commissions which Netrios collected and shared
with the WLEs.

        Red Acre, in conjunction with and in furtherance of Netrios’s operations, provided
customer support and customer relationship management (“CRM”). Red Acre managed the
customer onboarding and screening process as part of its CRM system. Red Acre aided
customers through the registration process, answered technical questions, and responded to
customer complaints. Red Acre also offered marketing services. Red Acre intentionally
performed these acts knowing that Netrios was facilitating off-exchange leveraged or margined
retail commodity transactions involving non-ECP U.S. customers.

      As of September 30, 2025, Respondents ceased business activities related to leveraged or
margined retail commodity transactions.

                                  III.    LEGAL DISCUSSION

A.      Netrios Engaged in Unlawful Off-Exchange Leveraged or Margined Retail
        Commodity Transactions in Violation of Section 4(a) of the Act

        Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. § 2(c)(2)(D), applies to “any agreement, contract,
or transaction in any commodity that is . . . entered into with, or offered to (even if not entered
into with), a [non-ECP] . . . on a leveraged or margined basis” and which does not result in actual
delivery within 28 days (hereafter, “leveraged or margined retail commodity transactions”).
Section 2(c)(2)(D)(i), (ii)(III)(aa) of the Act, 7 U.S.C § 2(c)(2)(D)(i), (ii)(III)(aa). Section 4(a) of
the Act, 7 U.S.C. § 6(a), applies to leveraged or margined retail commodity transactions as if
those transactions were contracts of sale of a commodity for future delivery. Section
2(c)(2)(D)(iii) of the Act, 7 U.S.C § 2(c)(2)(D)(iii).



                                                   3

       Cryptocurrencies traded on the WLE’s branded platforms are “commodities” under the
Act. See, e.g., United States v. Reed, No. 20-cr-500 (JGK), 2022 WL 597180, at *3-5 (S.D.N.Y.
Feb. 28, 2022); CFTC v. McDonnell, 287 F. Supp. 3d 213, 228-29 (E.D.N.Y. 2018); In re
Coinflip, Inc., CFTC No. 15-29, 2015 WL 5535736, at *2 (Sept. 17, 2015).

        Section 4(a) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. § 6(a), in relevant part, makes it unlawful for any person
to offer to enter into, enter into, execute, confirm the execution of, or conduct an office or
business in the United States for the purpose of soliciting or accepting any order for, or otherwise
dealing in, any transaction in, or in connection with, a contract for the purchase or sale of a
commodity for future delivery, unless such transaction is made on or subject to the rules of a
board of trade that has been designated or registered by the CFTC as a contract market for the
specific commodity (i.e., a DCM). See, e.g., In re Young Scott & Associates, LLC, CFTC No.
14-27, 2014 WL 4793546, at *3-4 (Sept. 23, 2014).

        During the Relevant Period, Netrios provided technology and infrastructure to the WLEs
so that they could offer and sell to non-ECP U.S. customers leveraged or margined retail
commodity transactions involving forex, metals, and cryptocurrencies. By facilitating these off-
exchange trades, Netrios offered to enter into, entered into, executed, confirmed the execution of,
and/or conducted business in the United States for the purpose of soliciting and/or accepting
orders for, and/or otherwise dealing in, leveraged or margined retail commodity transactions with
non-ECP U.S. residents that did not result in actual delivery within 28 days. These leveraged or
margined retail commodity transactions were not conducted on or subject to the rules of a board
of trade that has been designated or registered by the CFTC as a contract market. Thus, Netrios
violated Section 4(a) of the Act.

B.     Red Acre Aided and Abetted Netrios’s Violation of Section 4(a) of the Act

        Section 13(a) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. § 13c(a), states that any person who willfully aids,
abets, counsels, commands, induces, or procures the commission of a violation of any of the
provisions of the Act, or any of the rules, regulations or orders issued pursuant to the Act, may be
held responsible for such violation as a principal. Liability as an aider and abettor requires proof
that: (1) the Act was violated; (2) the aider and abettor had knowledge of the wrongdoing
underlying the violation; and (3) the aider and abettor intentionally assisted the primary
wrongdoer. See In re Societe Generale S.A., CFTC No. 18-14, 2018 WL 2761752, at *45 (June
4, 2018) (citing In re Nikkhah, CFTC No. 95-13, 2000 WL 622872, at *11 n.28 (May 12, 2000)).
Although actual knowledge of the primary wrongdoer’s conduct is required, knowledge of the
unlawfulness of such conduct need not be demonstrated. See id. (citing In re Lincolnwood
Commodities, Inc., CFTC No. 78-48, 1984 WL 48104, at *28 (Jan. 31, 1984)). Knowing
assistance can be inferred from the surrounding facts and circumstances. See id. (citing
Lincolnwood Commodities, 1984 WL 48104, at *29).

        Red Acre aided and abetted Netrios’s facilitation of off-exchange trades in leveraged or
margined retail commodity transactions to non-ECP U.S. customers in violation of Section 4(a)
of the Act. Red Acre knew of and intentionally aided and abetted Netrios’s efforts to conduct
leveraged or margined retail commodity transactions to non-ECP U.S. customers by providing
customer and technical support to WLE customers, including non-ECP U.S. customers, as well
as marketing services. Accordingly, pursuant to Section 13(a) of the Act, Red Acre aided and
                                                 4

abetted and is therefore liable for Netrios’s violations of Section 4(a) of the Act. See, e.g., CFTC
v. Lim, 2023 WL 11984840 (N.D. Ill. Dec. 14, 2023) (finding defendant liable for aiding and
abetting violation of Section 4(a) in consent order); In re Farmers Cooperative Co., CFTC No.
99-6, 2000 WL 36696331 (Mar. 9, 2000) (same).

                             IV.     FINDINGS OF VIOLATIONS

        Based on the foregoing, the Commission finds that, during the Relevant Period, Netrios
violated Section 4(a) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. § 6(a), and Red Acre aided and abetted Netrios’s
violations of that provision pursuant to Section 13(a) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. § 13c(a).

                              V.      OFFER OF SETTLEMENT

       Respondents have submitted the Offer in which they, without admitting the findings and
conclusions herein:

A.     Acknowledge service of this Order;

B.     Admit the jurisdiction of the Commission with respect to all matters set forth in this
       Order and for any action or proceeding brought or authorized by the Commission based
       on violation of or enforcement of this Order;

C.     Waive:

       1.       The filing and service of a complaint and notice of hearing;

       2.       A hearing;

       3.       All post-hearing procedures;

       4.       Judicial review by any court;

       5.       Any and all rights or defenses Respondents have or might have for the matter to
                be adjudicated in a federal district court in the first instance, including any
                associated right to a jury trial;

       6.       Any and all objections to the participation by any member of the Commission’s
                staff in the Commission’s consideration of the Offer;

       7.       Any and all claims that they may possess under the Equal Access to Justice Act, 5
                U.S.C. § 504, and 28 U.S.C. § 2412, and/or the rules promulgated by the
                Commission in conformity therewith, Part 148 of the Regulations, 17 C.F.R. pt.
                148 (2025), relating to, or arising from, this proceeding;

       8.       Any and all claims that they may possess under the Small Business Regulatory
                Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, Pub. L. No. 104-121, tit. II, §§ 201–253, 110
                                                 5

            Stat. 847, 857–74 (codified as amended at 28 U.S.C. § 2412 and in scattered
            sections of 5 U.S.C. and 15 U.S.C.), relating to, or arising from, this proceeding;
            and

     9.     Any claims of Double Jeopardy based on the institution of this proceeding or the
            entry in this proceeding of any order imposing a civil monetary penalty or any
            other relief, including this Order;

D.   Stipulate that the record basis on which this Order is entered shall consist solely of the
     findings contained in this Order to which Respondents have consented in the Offer;

E.   Consent, solely on the basis of the Offer, to the Commission’s entry of this Order that:

     1.     Makes findings by the Commission that Netrios violated Section 4(a) of the Act, 7
            U.S.C. § 6(a), and Red Acre aided and abetted Netrios’s violation of that
            provision pursuant to Section 13(a) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. § 13c(a);

     2.     Orders Respondents to cease and desist from violating Section 4(a) of the Act;

     3.     Orders Netrios to pay a civil monetary penalty in the amount of one million seven
            hundred fifty thousand dollars ($1,750,000) within ten (10) days of the date of
            entry of this Order, plus post-judgment interest in the event such civil monetary
            penalty is not paid within ten days of the date of entry of this Order;

     4.     Orders Red Acre to pay a civil monetary penalty in the amount of seven hundred
            fifty thousand dollars ($750,000) within ten (10) days of the date of entry of this
            Order, plus post-judgment interest in the event such civil monetary penalty is not
            paid within ten days of the date of entry of this Order;

     5.     Orders Respondents and any of their successors and assigns to comply with the
            conditions and undertakings consented to in the Offer and as set forth in Part VI
            of this Order.

     Upon consideration, the Commission has determined to accept the Offer.

                                       VI.     ORDER

Accordingly, IT IS HEREBY ORDERED THAT:

1.   Respondents and any of their successors and assigns shall cease and desist from violating
     Section 4(a) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. § 6(a).

2.   Netrios shall pay a civil monetary penalty in the amount of one million seven hundred

     the amount of seven hundred fifty thousand dollars ($750,000) (collectively, the “CMP
     Obligations”), within ten (10) days of the date of the entry of this Order. If the CMP

            ORDER INSTITUTING PROCEEDINGS PURSUANT TO
     SECTION 6(c) AND (d) OF THE COMMODITY EXCHANGE ACT, MAKING
             FINDINGS, AND IMPOSING REMEDIAL SANCTIONS

                                  I.      INTRODUCTION

        The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“Commission”) has reason to believe that
from at least January 2021 to the present (“Relevant Period”), Banco Santander, S.A. (“BSSA”)
and Santander US Capital Markets LLC (“SanCap”) (collectively, “Respondents”) violated, as
set forth below, Sections 4g, 4s(f)(1)(B), 4s(g)(1), and 4s(h)(1)(B) of the Commodity Exchange
Act (“Act”), 7 U.S.C. §§ 6g, 6s(f)(1)(B), 6s(g)(1), 6s(h)(1)(B), and Commission Regulations
(“Regulations”) 1.35(a)(1)(i) and (iii), 23.201(a)(1), 23.202(a)(1) and (b)(1), 23.602(a), and
166.3, 17 C.F.R. §§ 1.35(a)(1)(i), (iii), 23.201(a)(1), 23.202(a)(1), (b)(1), 23.602(a), 166.3
(2024). Therefore, the Commission deems it appropriate and in the public interest that public
administrative proceedings be, and hereby are, instituted to determine whether Respondents
engaged in the violations set forth herein and to determine whether any order should be issued
imposing remedial sanctions.

        In anticipation of the institution of an administrative proceeding, Respondents have
submitted an Offer of Settlement (“Offer”), which the Commission has determined to accept.
Without admitting or denying any of the findings or conclusions herein, Respondents consent to
the entry of this Order Instituting Proceedings Pursuant to Section 6(c) and (d) of the Commodity

Exchange Act, Making Findings, and Imposing Remedial Sanctions (“Order”), and acknowledge
service of this Order. 1

                                                II.      FINDINGS

The Commission finds the following:

A.       Summary

        During the Relevant Period, Respondents’ employees communicated using unapproved
methods. These written communications were sent and received by Respondents’ employees
and included messages related to Respondents’ businesses as Commission registrants that were
required to be maintained under Commission-mandated recordkeeping requirements. These
written communications were not captured and preserved by Respondents. As a result,
Respondents violated, as set forth below, Sections 4g, 4s(f)(1)(B), and 4s(g)(1) of the Act, 7
U.S.C. §§ 6g, 6s(f)(1)(B), 6s(g)(1), and Regulations 1.35, 23.201(a)(1), and 23.202(a)(1) and
(b)(1), 17 C.F.R. §§ 1.35(a)(1)(i) and (iii), 23.201(a)(1), 23.202(a)(1), (b)(1) (2024). In addition,
the use of unauthorized communication methods violated Respondents’ policies and procedures,
which prohibited such communications. Respondents did not implement a diligent supervisory
system to ensure compliance with Commission recordkeeping requirements and Respondents’
own policies and procedures, and therefore, Respondents failed to diligently supervise matters
related to Respondents’ businesses as Commission registrants in violation of Section 4s(h)(1)(B)
of the Act, 7 U.S.C. § 6s(h)(1)(B), and Regulations 23.602(a) and 166.3, 17 C.F.R. §§ 23.602(a),
166.3 (2024), as set forth below.

        In accepting Respondents’ Offer, the Commission recognizes Respondents’ exemplary
cooperation. The Commission’s recognition is reflected in a reduced penalty, with Respondents
receiving the maximum cooperation mitigation credit toward the full monetary penalty
appropriate for these violations.

B.       Respondents

       Banco Santander, S.A. is a financial services company with its headquarters in Madrid,
Spain. BSSA has been registered with the Commission as a non-U.S. swap dealer since July
2013.

       Santander US Capital Markets LLC is a Delaware limited liability company with its
headquarters in New York, New York. SanCap is an indirect wholly owned subsidiary of BSSA.
SanCap has been registered with the Commission as a futures commission merchant (“FCM”)
since February 2023, having been established through the merger of Santander Investment

1
  Respondents consent to the use of the findings of fact and conclusions of law in this Order in this proceeding and
in any other proceeding brought by the Commission or to which the Commission is a party or claimant and agree
that they shall be taken as true and correct and given preclusive effect therein, without further proof. Respondents
do not consent, however, to the use of this Order, or the findings or conclusions herein, as the sole basis for any
other proceeding brought by the Commission or to which the Commission is a party or claimant, other than: a
proceeding in bankruptcy or receivership; or a proceeding to enforce the terms of this Order. Respondents do not
consent to the use of the Offer or this Order, or the findings or conclusions in this Order, by any other party in any
other proceeding.


                                                           2

Securities Inc. (“SIS”) and Amherst Pierpont Securities LLC (“APS”). SIS was registered with
the Commission as an FCM from March 2008 until March 2023. APS was registered with the
Commission as an introducing broker from January 2012 through May 2021. 2

C.      Facts

        Although Respondents’ policies and procedures prohibited the use of unapproved
communication methods, during the Relevant Period, Respondents’ employees engaged in
written communications related to Respondents’ Commission-regulated businesses that were not
monitored, captured, or preserved. Further, although no customer or market harm is known to
have occurred as a result, Commission recordkeeping requirements were not met, and
Respondents failed to diligently supervise their employees to ensure compliance.

        1.       Respondents’ Recordkeeping Failures

        During the Relevant Period, Respondents’ policies and procedures prohibited employees
from using unapproved communication methods, such as personal text messages, to engage in
business-related communications. Additionally, Respondents provided annual training and
regularly issued compliance bulletins regarding their communications policies.

        Messages sent through Respondents’ approved communication methods were monitored,
subject to review, and when appropriate, archived. However, messages sent using unapproved
communication methods, including over personal text messages, were not monitored, subject to
review, or archived.

        A sampling analysis conducted by Respondents, which included the personal devices of
approximately five percent of its U.S.-based associated persons (“APs”) over a six-month period
in 2021, revealed that all of the sampled APs violated Respondents’ communications policies
and procedures by using personal text messages to communicate with coworkers and/or market
participants about business activities. The analysis further revealed that the communications of
some of these sampled APs involved Respondents’ Commission-regulated businesses.
Respondents acknowledge that these results are likely representative of the issue more broadly.

        2.       Exemplary Cooperation

        Respondents cooperated with the Division of Enforcement (“Division”) throughout its
investigation. Respondents voluntarily collected and reviewed messages retrieved from the
personal devices of a sampling of Respondents’ APs and made presentations to Division staff
regarding Respondents’ Commission-regulated businesses, their electronic communications
compliance program, and the results of the sampling review.

        As part of their cooperation efforts, Respondents have significantly completed
remediation. Respondents undertook an internal review to identify and assess the scope of
potential violative communications. Respondents represent that they have enhanced their
policies and procedures, increased training concerning the use of unapproved communication

2
 References to “SanCap” herein include both SIS and APS, as appropriate, for the respective timeframes within the
Relevant Period each was in existence.


                                                        3

methods, enhanced their surveillance efforts to mitigate the risk of employees engaging in
communications using unapproved communication methods, including on personal devices, and
have been implementing significant changes to the technology available to their personnel.
Further, Respondents represent that an internal audit of Respondents’ Commission-regulated
U.S. businesses is being conducted to further review and assess Respondents’ electronic
communications compliance program, including their surveillance controls and processes.

                                   III.    LEGAL DISCUSSION

A.      BSSA Failed to Keep Required Records in Violation of Sections 4s(f)(1)(B) and
        4s(g)(1) of the Act and Regulations 23.201(a) and 23.202(a)(1) and (b)(1).

         Section 4s(f)(1)(B) of the Act obligates a swap dealer to keep “books and records of all
activities related to its business as a swap dealer . . . in such form and manner and for such period
as may be prescribed by the Commission by rule or regulation.” 7 U.S.C. § 6s(f)(1)(B); see also
Section 4s(g)(1) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. § 6s(g)(1) (requiring swap dealers to maintain daily trading
records). Part 23 of the Regulations implement these recordkeeping requirements. 17 C.F.R. pt.
23 (2024).

         Pursuant to Regulation 23.201(a)(1), a swap dealer is required to “keep full, complete,
and systematic records, together with all pertinent data and memoranda, of all its swaps
activities,” including “[r]ecords of each transaction, including all documents on which
transaction information is originally recorded.” 17 C.F.R. § 23.201(a)(1) (2024). Further,
Regulation 23.202(a)(1) and (b)(1) requires, among other things, that a swap dealer keep daily
trading records of all swaps and related cash and forward transactions it executes, including,
specifically, a record of all oral and written communications provided or received concerning
quotes, solicitations, bids, offers, instructions, trading, and prices that led to the execution of a
swap transaction or the conclusion of a related cash or forward transactions. 17 C.F.R. §
23.202(a)(1), (b)(1).

       During the Relevant Period, as a result of its employees’ use of unapproved
communication methods, BSSA violated Sections 4s(f)(1)(B) and 4s(g)(1) of the Act and
Regulations 23.201(a)(1) and 23.202(a)(1) and (b)(1).

B.      SanCap Failed to Keep Required Records in Violation of Section 4g of the Act and
        Regulation 1.35(a)(1)(i) and (iii).

        Section 4g of the Act requires FCMs and other registrants to create and keep books and
records pertaining to transactions and positions in commodities for future delivery and in any
significant price discovery contract in such form and manner and for such period as may be
required by the Commission. 7 U.S.C. § 6g (2024). Regulation 1.35(a)(1), 17 C.F.R. § 1.35
(a)(1) (2024), sets forth some of the books and records that are required to be kept and
maintained by FCMs. Specifically, an FCM must:

        (i) Keep full, complete, and systematic records . . . of all transactions relating to
        its business of dealing in commodity interests and related cash and forward
        transactions, which shall include all orders (filled, unfilled, or canceled), . . . and



                                                   4

       all other records, which have been prepared in the course of its business of
       dealing in commodity interests and related cash or forward transactions . . . ;

                                       *       *       *

       (iii) Keep all oral and written communications provided or received concerning
       quotes, solicitations, bids, offers, instructions, trading, and prices that lead to the
       execution of a transaction in a commodity interest, and in any related cash or
       forward transactions . . . .

       During the Relevant Period, as a result of its employees’ use of unapproved
communication methods, SanCap violated Section 4g of the Act and Regulation 1.35(a)(1)(i) and
(iii).

       C.      Respondents Failed to Diligently Supervise.

       Regulation 166.3 states:

       Each Commission registrant, except an associated person who has no supervisory
       duties, must diligently supervise the handling by its partners, officers, employees
       and agents (or persons occupying a similar status or performing a similar
       function) of all commodity interest accounts carried, operated, advised or
       introduced by the registrant and all other activities of its partners, officers,
       employees and agents (or persons occupying a similar status or performing a
       similar function) relating to its business as a Commission registrant.

17 C.F.R. § 166.3 (2024).

        A violation of Regulation 166.3 is demonstrated by showing either that: (1) the
registrant’s supervisory system was generally inadequate; or (2) the registrant failed to perform
its supervisory duties diligently. In the Matter of Murlas Commodities, Inc., CFTC No. 85-29,
1995 WL 523563, at *9 (Sept. 1, 1995) (consent order); In re GNP Commodities, Inc., CFTC
No. 89-1, 1992 WL 201158, at *17-19 (Aug. 11, 1992) (consent order) (providing that, even if
an adequate supervisory system is in place, Regulation 166.3 can still be violated if the
supervisory system is not diligently administered); Sansom Refining Co. v. Drexel Burnham
Lambert, Inc., CFTC No. 82-R448, 1990 WL 282783, at *11 (Feb. 16, 1990) (consent order)
(noting that, under Regulation 166.3, registrants have a “duty to develop procedures for the
detection and deterrence of possible wrongdoing by [their] agents” (internal quotation omitted));
see also In re Rosenthal Collins Grp., LLC, CFTC No. 12-18, 2012 WL 1242406, at *6 (Apr. 12,
2012) (consent order) (finding that respondent failed to perform supervisory duties diligently by
not following its compliance procedures that were in place). A violation under Regulation 166.3
is an independent violation for which no underlying violation is necessary. See In the Matter of
Thomas Collins, CFTC No. 94-13, 1997 WL 761927, at *10 (Dec. 10, 1997) (consent order).
Evidence of violations that “should be detected by a diligent system of supervision, either
because of the nature of the violations or because the violations have occurred repeatedly” is
probative of a failure to diligently supervise. In the Matter of Paragon Futures Ass’n, CFTC No.
88-18, 1992 WL 74261, at *14 (April 1, 1992) (consent order) (“The focus of any proceeding to



                                                   5

determine whether Rule 166.3 has been violated will be on whether [a] review [has] occurred
and, if it did, whether it was ‘diligent.’”).

        Section 4s(h)(1)(B) of the Act, requires “diligent supervision of the business of the
registered swap dealer.” 7 U.S.C. § 6s(h)(1)(B). The Regulations require that each swap dealer
“establish and maintain a system to supervise, and shall diligently supervise, all activities
relating to its business performed by its partners, members, officers, employees, and agents (or
persons occupying a similar status or performing a similar function).” Regulation 23.602(a), 17
C.F.R. § 23.602(a) (2024). The operative language of Regulation 23.602(a) is similar to the
language of the Commission’s longstanding supervision regulation for futures and options,
Regulation 166.3, 17 C.F.R. § 166.3 (2024). In re Commerzbank AG, CFTC No. 1903, 2018 WL
5921385, at *10-11 (Nov. 8, 2018) (consent order) (noting textual similarities between
Regulation 23.602 and Regulation 166.3 and applying case law concerning Regulation 166.3).

        During the Relevant Period, SanCap failed to supervise its FCM activities diligently, and
BSSA failed to supervise its swap dealer business activities diligently. Respondents failed to
maintain adequate supervisory systems to ensure that their employees complied with
Commission recordkeeping requirements and Respondents’ policies and procedures that
prohibited business-related communications on unapproved communication methods.
Respondents’ failures to diligently supervise are demonstrated by their failure to keep

               ORDER INSTITUTING PROCEEDINGS PURSUANT TO
        SECTION 6(c) AND (d) OF THE COMMODITY EXCHANGE ACT, MAKING
                FINDINGS, AND IMPOSING REMEDIAL SANCTIONS

                                           I.       INTRODUCTION

        The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“Commission”) has reason to believe that
from at least May 2019 to August 2023 (“Relevant Period”), SMBC Capital Markets, Inc.
(“Respondent”) violated, as set forth below, Sections 4s(f)(1)(B), 4s(g)(1), and 4s(h)(1)(B) of the
Commodity Exchange Act (“Act”), 7 U.S.C. §§ 6s(f)(1)(B), 6s(g)(1), 6s(h)(1)(B), and
Commission Regulations (“Regulations”) 23.201(a)(1), 23.202(a)(1) and (b)(1), and 23.602(a),
17 C.F.R. §§ 23.201(a)(1), 23.202(a)(1), (b)(1), 23.602(a) (2024). Therefore, the Commission
deems it appropriate and in the public interest that public administrative proceedings be, and
hereby are, instituted to determine whether Respondent engaged in the violations set forth herein
and to determine whether any order should be issued imposing remedial sanctions.

        In anticipation of the institution of an administrative proceeding, Respondent has
submitted an Offer of Settlement (“Offer”), which the Commission has determined to accept.
Without admitting or denying any of the findings or conclusions here, Respondent consents to
the entry of this Order Instituting Proceedings Pursuant to Section 6(c) and (d) of the Commodity
Exchange Act, Making Findings, and Imposing Remedial Sanctions (“Order”), and
acknowledges service of this Order.1


1
  Respondent consents to the use of the findings of fact and conclusions of law in this Order in this proceeding and
in any other proceeding brought by the Commission or to which the Commission is a party or claimant and agrees
that they shall be taken as true and correct and given preclusive effect therein, without further proof. Respondent
does not consent, however, to the use of this Order, or the findings or conclusions herein, as the sole basis for any
other proceeding brought by the Commission or to which the Commission is a party or claimant, other than: a
proceeding in bankruptcy or receivership; or a proceeding to enforce the terms of this Order. Respondent does not
consent to the use of the Offer or this Order, or the findings or conclusions in this Order, by any other party in any
other proceeding.

                                      II.     FINDINGS

The Commission finds the following:

A.     Summary

        During the Relevant Period, Respondent’s employees communicated using unapproved
methods. These written communications were sent and received by Respondent’s employees
and included messages related to Respondent’s business as a Commission registrant that were
required to be maintained under Commission-mandated recordkeeping requirements. These
written communications were not captured and preserved by Respondent. As a result,
Respondent violated Sections 4s(f)(1)(B) and 4s(g)(1) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. §§ 6s(f)(1)(B),
6s(g)(1), and Regulations 23.201(a)(1) and 23.202(a)(1) and (b)(1), 17 C.F.R. §§ 23.201(a)(1),
23.202(a)(1), (b)(1) (2024). In addition, the use of unauthorized communication methods
violated Respondent’s policies and procedures, which prohibited such communications.
Respondent did not implement a diligent supervisory system to ensure compliance with
Commission recordkeeping requirements and Respondent’s own policies and procedures, and
therefore Respondent failed to diligently supervise matters related to Respondent’s business as a
Commission registrant in violation of Section 4s(h)(1)(B) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. § 6s(h)(1)(B), and
Regulation 23.602(a), 17 C.F.R. § 23.602(a) (2024).

        In accepting Respondent’s Offer, the Commission recognizes Respondent’s exemplary
cooperation. The Commission’s recognition is reflected in a reduced penalty, with Respondent
receiving the maximum cooperation mitigation credit toward the full monetary penalty
appropriate for these violations.

B.     Respondent

       SMBC Capital Markets, Inc. is a financial services company with its headquarters in
New York, New York. Respondent has been registered with the Commission as a swap dealer
since December 31, 2012.

C.     Facts

        Although Respondent’s policies and procedures prohibited the use of unapproved
communication methods, during the Relevant Period, Respondent’s employees engaged in
written communications related to Respondent’s Commission-regulated business that were not
monitored, captured, or preserved. Further, although no customer or market harm is known to
have occurred as a result, Commission recordkeeping requirements were not met, and
Respondent failed to diligently supervise its employees to ensure compliance.

       1.      Respondent’s Recordkeeping Failures

       During the Relevant Period, Respondent’s policies and procedures prohibited employees
from using unapproved communication methods, such as personal text messages and WhatsApp,
to engage in business-related communications. Additionally, Respondent provided training to its
employees and issued policy reminders regarding Respondent’s communications policies.



                                                2

        Messages sent through Respondent’s approved communications methods were
monitored, subject to review, and when appropriate, archived. However, messages sent using
unapproved communication methods, including over personal WhatsApp, email, and text
messages, were not monitored, subject to review, or archived.

        In connection with the Division of Enforcement’s (“Division’s”) investigation,
Respondent conducted a review of its employees’ use of unapproved communications. This
review resulted in a determination that Respondent’s employees had used unapproved
communication methods to engage in firm business. A sampling analysis conducted by
Respondent, which included the personal devices of approximately ten percent of its associated
persons (“APs”) over at least a one-year period, revealed that approximately seventy percent of
the sampled APs violated Respondent’s communications policies and procedures by using
personal text messages or other unapproved methods to communicate with brokers, coworkers,
and/or market participants. The analysis further revealed that the communications of some of
these sampled APs involved Respondent’s Commission-regulated business. Respondent
acknowledges that these results are likely representative of the issue more broadly.

       2.      Exemplary Cooperation

       Respondent cooperated with the Division throughout its investigation. Respondent
voluntarily collected and reviewed messages retrieved from the personal devices of a sampling
of Respondent’s APs and made presentations to Division staff regarding, among other things,
Respondent’s Commission-regulated business and its electronic communications compliance
program.

        As part of its cooperation efforts, Respondent has completed remediation. Respondent
represents that it has enhanced its policies and procedures, provided new training concerning the
use of unapproved communication methods, approved new communication platforms to address
employee needs while ensuring compliance, implemented technological improvements, and
enhanced its disciplinary framework to mitigate the risk of employees communicating by
unapproved methods. Respondent further represents it disciplined staff that it found to have
violated its policies regarding unapproved communication methods.

                                 III.    LEGAL DISCUSSION

A.     Respondent Failed to Keep Required Records in Violation of Sections 4s(f)(1)(B)
       and 4s(g)(1) of the Act and Regulations 23.201(a) and 23.202(a)(1) and (b)(1).

        Section 4s(f)(1)(B) of the Act obligates a swap dealer to keep “books and records of all
activities related to its business as a swap dealer . . . in such form and manner and for such period
as may be prescribed by the Commission by rule or regulation.” 7 U.S.C. § 6s(f)(1)(B); see also
Section 4s(g)(1) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. § 6s(g)(1) (requiring swap dealers to maintain daily trading
records). Part 23 of the Regulations implement these recordkeeping requirements. 17 C.F.R. pt.
23 (2024).

        Pursuant to Regulation 23.201(a)(1), a swap dealer is required to “keep full, complete,
and systematic records, together with all pertinent data and memoranda, of all its swaps
activities,” including “[r]ecords of each transaction, including all documents on which


                                                 3

transaction information is originally recorded.” 17 C.F.R. § 23.201(a)(1) (2024). Further,
Regulation 23.202(a)(1) and (b)(1) requires, among other things, that a swap dealer keep daily
trading records of all swaps and related cash and forward transactions it executes, including,
specifically, a record of all oral and written communications provided or received concerning
quotes, solicitations, bids, offers, instructions, trading, and prices that led to the execution of a
swap transaction or the conclusion of a related cash or forward transactions. 17 C.F.R. §
23.202(a)(1), (b)(1).

       During the Relevant Period, as a result of its employees’ use of unapproved
communication methods, Respondent violated Sections 4s(f)(1)(B) and 4s(g)(1) of the Act and
Regulations 23.201(a) and 23.202(a)(1) and (b)(1).

B.      Respondent Failed to Diligently Supervise in Violation of Section 4s(h)(1)(B) of the
        Act and Regulation 23.602(a).

        Section 4s(h)(1)(B) requires “diligent supervision of the business of the registered swap
dealer[.]” 7 U.S.C. § 6s(h)(1)(B). Implementing this requirement, Regulation 23.602(a) requires
that each swap dealer “shall establish and maintain a system to supervise, and shall diligently
supervise, all activities relating to its business performed by its partners, members, officers,
employees, and agents (or persons occupying a similar status or performing a similar function).”
17 C.F.R. § 23.602(a) (2024). The operative language of Regulation 23.602 is similar to the
language of the Commission’s longstanding supervision regulation for futures and options,
Regulation 166.3, 17 C.F.R. § 166.3 (2024).

        Under Regulation 23.602(a), a violation is demonstrated by showing either that: (1) the
registrant’s supervisory system was generally inadequate; or (2) the registrant failed to perform
its supervisory duties diligently. See In re JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., CFTC No. 22-07, 2021
WL 6098347, at *6 (Dec. 17, 2021) (consent order); see also In re Commerzbank AG, CFTC No.
19-03, 2018 WL 5921385, at *10-11 (Nov. 8, 2018) (consent order) (noting textual similarities
between Regulation 23.602 and Regulation 166.3, applying case law concerning Regulation
166.3). Either showing “alone is sufficient to establish a violation of the supervision
requirement.” Id., at *10 (interpreting Regulation 23.602 in light of Regulation 166.3
precedents). No evidence of an underlying violation is necessary. In re Collins, CFTC No. 94-
13, 1997 WL 761927, at *10 (Dec. 10, 1997) (consent order) (interpreting Regulation 166.3).
Evidence of violations that “‘should be detected by a diligent system of supervision, either
because of the nature of the violations or because the violations have occurred repeatedly,’ is
probative of a failure to supervise.” See In re Bank of Nova Scotia, CFTC No. 20-26, 2020 WL
4926053, at *10 (Aug. 19, 2020) (consent order) (quoting In re Société Générale Int’l Ltd.,
CFTC No. 19-38, 2009 WL 4915485, at *7 (Sept. 30, 2019) (consent order)).

       Respondent failed to supervise its swap dealer business activities diligently during the
Relevant Period. Respondent failed to maintain an adequate supervisory system to ensure that its
employees complied with Commission recordkeeping requirements and Respondent’s policies
and procedures that prohibited business-related communications on unapproved communication
methods. Respondent’s failure to diligently supervise is demonstrated by its failure to keep
Commission-required records and to detect violations of its policies and procedures.



                                                   4

Accordingly, Respondent failed to supervise diligently its officers, employees, and agents, in
violation of Section 4s(h)(1)(B) of the Act and Regulation 23.602(a).

                            IV.     FINDINGS OF VIOLATIONS

        Based on the foregoing, the Commission finds that, during the Relevant Period,
Respondent violated Sections 4s(f)(1)(B), 4s(g)(1), and 4s(h)(1)(B) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. §§
6s(f)(1)(B), 6s(g)(1), 6s(h)(1)(B), and Regulations 23.201(a)(1), 23.202(a)(1) and (b)(1), and
23.602(a), 17 C.F.R. §§ 23.201(a)(1), 23.202(a)(1), (b)(1), 23.602(a) (2024).

                              V.     OFFER OF SETTLEMENT

       Respondent has submitted the Offer in which it:

A.     Consents to the resolution of this matter in an administrative proceeding.

B.     Acknowledges service of this Order;

C.     Admits the jurisdiction of the Commission with respect to all matters set forth in this
       Order and for any action or proceeding brought or authorized by the Commission based
       on violation of or enforcement of this Order;

D.     Waives:

       1.      The filing and service of a complaint and notice of hearing;

       2.      A hearing;

       3.      All post-hearing procedures;

       4.      Any and all rights or defenses that Respondent has or might have for the matter to
               be adjudicated in a federal district court in the first instance, including any
               associated right to a jury trial;

       5.      Judicial review by any court;

       6.      Any and all objections to the participation by any member of the Commission’s
               staff in the Commission’s consideration of the Offer;

       7.      Any and all claims that Respondent may possess under the Equal Access to
               Justice Act, 5 U.S.C. § 504, and 28 U.S.C. § 2412, and/or the rules promulgated
               by the Commission in conformity therewith, Part 148 of the Regulations, 17
               C.F.R. pt. 148 (2024), relating to, or arising from, this proceeding;

       8.      Any and all claims that Respondent may possess under the Small Business
               Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, Pub. L. No. 104-121, tit. II, §§
               201-253, 110 Stat. 847, 857-74 (codified as amended at 28 U.S.C. § 2412 and in
               scattered sections of 5 U.S.C. and 15 U.S.C.), relating to, or arising from, this
               proceeding; and


                                                5

     9.     Any claims of Double Jeopardy based on the institution of this proceeding or the
            entry in this proceeding of any order imposing a civil monetary penalty or any
            other relief, including this Order;

E.   Agrees that Respondent is not the prevailing party in this action for purposes of the
     waiver of any and all rights under the Equal Access to Justice Act specified in Paragraph
     D.7 above.

F.   Stipulates that the record basis on which this Order is entered shall consist solely of the
     findings contained in this Order to which Respondent has consented in the Offer;

G.   Consents, solely on the basis of the Offer, to the Commission’s entry of this Order that:

     1.     Makes findings by the Commission that Respondent violated Sections 4s(f)(1)(B),
            4s(g)(1), and 4s(h)(1)(B) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. §§ 6s(f)(1)(B), 6s(g)(1),
            6s(h)(1)(B), and Regulations 23.201(a)(1), 23.202(a)(1) and (b)(1), and 23.602(a),
            17 C.F.R. §§ 23.201(a)(1), 23.202(a)(1), (b)(1), 23.602(a) (2024);

     2.     Orders Respondent to cease and desist from violating Sections 4s(f)(1)(B),
            4s(g)(1), and 4s(h)(1)(B) of the Act, and Regulations 23.201(a)(1), 23.202(a)(1)
            and (b)(1), and 23.602(a);

     3.     Orders Respondent to pay a civil monetary penalty in the amount of five hundred
            thousand dollars ($500,000), plus post-judgment interest within fourteen (14)
            calendar days of the date of entry of this Order; and

     4.     Orders Respondent and its successors and assigns to comply with the conditions
            and undertakings consented to in the Offer and as set forth in Part VI of this
            Order.

H.   Represents that Respondent enhanced its policies and procedures, provided new training
     concerning the use of unapproved communication methods, approved new
     communication platforms to address employee needs while ensuring compliance,
     implemented technological improvements, enhanced its disciplinary framework to
     mitigate the risk of employees communicating by unapproved methods, and has
     disciplined staff it found to have violated its policies regarding unapproved
     communication methods.

     Upon consideration, the Commission has determined to accept the Offer.

                                       VI.     ORDER

     Accordingly, IT IS HEREBY ORDERED THAT:

A.   Respondent and its successors and assigns shall cease and desist from violating Sections

     6s(h)(1)(B), and Regulations 23.201(a)(1), 23.202(a)(1) and (b)(1), and 23.602(a), 17
     C.F.R. §§ 23.201(a)(1), 23.202(a)(1), (b)(1), 23.602(a) (2024).


                                               6

B.   Respondent shall pay a civil monetary penalty in the amount of five hundred thousand
